Looked at like that, it's clear that the bellicose impulses of Wilhelm II were based on the chivalry and weaponry of a vastly earlier age. The mistake was thinking he could win an offensive war. Worth clarifying that an expired US visa is not the same as expired immigration status (common misconception). USCIS considers visa as an entry permit; legality of stay is determined by immigration status, which can coincide with the visa validity period. However, for many non-immigrant visa categories, including, but not limited to F-1 (student), H-1B (business), H-4 (spouse/dependent), etc., valid immigration status often exceeds visa validity. Having a valid status with expired visa simply means that a new visa stamp would be required for re-entry.

In other words, being out-of-status is considered as illegal presence, having an expired visa is not.

Thank you for your reporting!

The one that made me chuckle was "interval training".  Back in the '90's, I used to Lindy hop 4 or 5 nights a week.  It's the perfect interval training with a 4 minute song that increases your heart rate and sweat rate, fast movement, jumping, kicking, and (of course) hopping.  This would be followed by a slow song or taking a break to catch your breath.  Repeat for three hours.
What made me chuckle is that I recently read that partner dancing will help prevent dementia and help one age well because it is physical as well as mental.  I told this to my dance partner from those days and said "Who knew we were aging well??  We thought we were just having fun!!"  (N.B. I still do Lindy hop, but not nearly as often...)

Regular exercise, either aerobic or HIIT, is a positive step towards better health. At first you can literally feel the strength and muscle you will need to do this, and then the next thing you know, you feel the muscular, the agility and the cardio strength that you did not have before. The phrase at the end - "Even if France is contributing relatively little to global greenhouse gas emissions...." - has become so familiar over the past 40 years, with the names of different countries, states, provinces, and cities interchangeable with "France".  Most often, it is as the most ludicrous of excuses for failing to take action on climate change.  Since I live in Canada, I most often hear it about this country, since our small population means that we can't contribute as much CO2 to the atmosphere as big countries like China and the USA.  We do, on the other hand, have one of the world's very highest per-capita levels of GHGs, so it is particularly cringeworthy when people argue that Canada shouldn't try to reduce our GHG emissions because they are small compared to those of China and USA.
The fact is that we were only able to destabilize Earth's climate by all of us working together, with every automobile ride, every overseas vacation, every meal cooked on a gas-fired stove, and every decision to have more than two children all contributing to the current crisis.  We all have an equal responsibility to try to fix the problem, no matter where we live.

Our days became far more manageable when we could cool our legs and splash water on our arms - our 5 year old completely drenched himself every time we saw one and he was in a better mood than in any other place we visited because of it. It was used by everyone (especially kids in the evening, where it became a full park with families picnicing while kids in their undies splashed). Everywhere else we went - Paris, Brittany and the Alps - where far more uncomfortable for us unless we found our way to a lake or beach (something people working in a city cannot afford to take time for in their day). These urban fountains were playful, pretty, and served a truly meaningful purpose in helping locals and tourists cool off.

I have a question about the risks associated with this procedure.  Doing the math (?), it looks to me like a woman's risk of developing this most deadly kind of cancer, starting in the fallopian tubes, is 0.88 percent (lifetime).  It is being offered in the context of hernia surgery, etc., and I see various estimates of the risks of serious complications from hernia surgery.  The thought does suggest itself that someone might elect to have her fallopian tubes removed even if she is not already getting some other kind of surgery.  So, two questions: (1) how much does having one's fallopian tubes removed increase the risk of serious complications or death beyond what one already has with the concomitant surgery, and (2) what is the risk of serious complications or death if you're just doing this not in the context of some other kind of surgery?

I know it says, "Is it safe to remove tubes? (Yes.)," but I would just like to press for a bit more information, since removing tubes in the context of hernia surgery (etc.), which is the main focus of the article, does seem to carry risks with it, and they are not (as far as I saw) mentioned in the article.

I think you have to know what those risks are in order to compare with the expected benefit, which is reducing a risk of 0.88 percent to near zero, presumably.

Those cases represent limitations on the severity of punishment relative to the offender’s culpability (i.e., limitations based on proportionality).

Europe Is burning—and the fastest fire extinguisher is methane reduction. 
The scenes from this summer should end the debate. European climate policy needs to change what it is optimizing for. For a quarter century, tge EU has organized its entire climate architecture around carbon dioxide— emission trading system allowances, 2050 net-zero targets, combustion-engine phase-outs, industrial decarbonization roadmaps. Every one of those instruments is aimed at the back half of the century. None of them will cool a single August between now and 2040. CO₂ that Europe eliminates in 2027 shows up in the temperature record decades later, because CO₂ persists in the atmosphere for centuries. That is a fact of atmospheric chemistry, not a talking point.

Methane is the opposite molecule. It is roughly 80 times more potent than CO₂ over a 20-year horizon and it clears the atmosphere in about 12 years. It is responsible for nearly one-third — about 0.5 °C — of the warming already realized. Cut methane hard this decade, and the temperature response is measurable within a decade. The IEA and the Climate and Clean Air Coalition put the achievable relief at roughly 0.2–0.3 °C by mid-century — the difference, in southern Europe, between a bad fire year and a catastrophic one.

If Europe is serious about protecting the citizens it evacuated this month, methane is the only climate lever whose timeline matches the crisis.

For those with health problems, a focus on standard treatments is beneficial.  The use of health trackers and new screening technologies is of unproven benefit.  Their use in a generally healthy population subset (those who pay the most attention to their health) will yield a lot of harmful false positives and unnecessary treatments, a lot of cost, a lot of anxiety, and also some true benefits.  The key question is where does the balance lie.  It's hard for the public to understand the statistics behind most studies, especially selection bias.  If the population being studied is very healthy or motivated, the outcomes will be misleadingly good.

You need to follow your instincts.

Sometimes the sky helps you out.  In the mountains, or the midwest, if clouds are getting rapidly taller, it’s time to get to shelter.

If in 30 minutes, the sky looks like the dress rehearsal for the second coming, believe it.

At other times, the Calm Before the Storm is literal.

A year ago, I was introduced to the book “Blow the Man Down”,  by the mixed-race son of a common seaman, taught his letters by a neighbor, who in the early 20s published a memoir of 40 years at the end of the square rigger - likely the finest such account extant (recently, amazingly, released on Kindle)

Multiple times he describes an eerily calm, which in a few hours turned into a typhoon, and the superhuman effort required to sail through it (or not:  twice his ship sank under him, once marooning him for three months.)

My great grandfather experienced something similar, walking out the back door on a still January South Dakota morning, only to see a white line on the horizon moving at 60 mph.  It hit before he made it to the house, as he walked into the midwestern blizzard of 1888, the temperature dropping 60 degrees in 15 minutes, in an absolute white-out.  He forced himself to keep walking in a storm that claimed hundreds, finally bumping into a masonry wall he had built, and followed home with his eyes frozen shut.

Pay attention to weather reports, but also trust your gut, especially about thunderstorms or flash floods hard to predict.

Weather is an oft used example of a chaotic system - one in which a small change in conditions can result in large changes in the overall weather. There is no way to overcome chaos with better instruments or bigger computers. So what scientists do with such systems is run all the variations of small changes and get an envelope of possible outcomes. That envelope allows a weather forecast to state the likelihood of corner-case outcomes. If you look at NOAA/NWS forecasts there will be watered-down language on likelihood of particularly bad outcomes. 

So my advice is to not buy better instruments, but use NOAA/NWS forecasts, and read the "Discussion" section and pay attention to what it says. Link: https://www.weather.gov/

This AI debate brings to mind Michael Crichton’s Jurassic Park. InGen’s scientists believed they had mastered prehistoric biology simply because they had extracted fragmented DNA from mosquitoes trapped in ancient amber. They built computer algorithms to monitor the island, assuming historical input was sufficient to predict behavior.

​As Ian Malcolm warned, relying on past data approximations to control dynamic, chaotic systems is a fatal flaw.

​Training AI weather models strictly on past satellite data is modern amber-analyzing. It shows how the system behaved under known conditions, but climate change is pushing us into uncharted territory.

​When confronted with unprecedented "gray swan" events, pattern-recognition tools fail where physics-based models hold. Just as InGen’s system failed because it couldn't imagine wild breeding, AI risks missing extreme storms simply because it has never seen them before. Data extrapolation is useful, but it is no substitute for physical realities.

comments.name: Andrew Szakmary
comments.body: I would like to offer a brief commentary on Irving Fisher and his “permanent plateau” statement made October 15, 1929. Yes, his timing was awful. Had you bought a value-weighted index of all listed U.S. stocks and reinvested the dividends, every one dollar invested at the end of September, 1929 would have been worth only 20 cents by the end of June 1932 (the depression low). However, at least in the past, the stock market has always recovered, and if you held those stocks for 30 years, by September 1959, each dollar invested would have grown to roughly $8.74, and you would have earned a respectable annual return of 7.49% in nominal terms and 5.62% in inflation-adjusted terms. So you would have done OK in the longer run despite the awful timing of your purchase, and the spirit of what Fisher said - that the stock market is a reasonable place to invest despite huge recent increases in stock prices - was not necessarily wrong. This episode may well hold valuable lessons for the current moment.

comments.name: gr8bkset
comments.body: In our car dependent cities, half of the land is dedicated to transportation infrastructure.  Many buildings require parking that is 3x-4x that of the building itself.  Our single family homes' living space only occupies 20% of the lot size while the 80% non living space consist of the garage, driveway, front and backyard. This inefficient use of land, aka sprawl, resulted in many cities having run out of land, so housing start at $1M. Even though we are car dependent, our automobiles sit unused 23hours (96%)  a day and takes up parking space at home and work.  This can be reversed by cities working with big employers to convert parking lots of large workplaces to dense affordable mixed use housing for those that work nearby.  Residents in these 5-minute communities give up the car, commute, garage, driveway, individual yards in favor of a shared pool of vehicles and common greenspaces. The more efficient use of space as well as not owning a car makes these communities affordable and not need subsidizing.  The "other" spouse can give up his/her commute and the car and work in support services of these communities.  Cities save from infrastructure costs and the environment save from less resources and emissions.  With less resource needs, residents need lower incomes and their jobs are less susceptible to outsourcing, automation and AI'd.

My first reaction was the same as Philip’s: “This was not your story to tell.” And I think that is the correct answer to the question about *etiquette.* (From that perspective it was rude of the twins to put their sibling on the spot when they could have just done their own genetic testing.) 

However, there is also an ethical dimension to this question. Do the twins have a right to whatever information is available? Does disclosure of hearsay harm anyone? (I hope *Ask the Ethicist* will respond to a letter like this too.)

I also agree with Phillip’s analysis of the ethical dimension. They did no harm and were not unethical. 

Is the other sibling upset about the etiquette or the ethics? We don’t know. But we do know that one could view these same facts from many different angles.

I spent a few fall and winter months in a rural town in Himachal Pradesh. I witnessed children unable to go to school because there was no heat or electricity in their snowy foothill schools. When they did attend class, they spent half their time in the woods collecting sticks for fires to heat the room. Teachers showed up and did their best with their pitiful resources.

A newly married couple from Bihar, who by pluck and householder’s skills, found employment and housing in my large bed and breakfast for foreigners cheerfully greeted us at each meal. Their happiness was infectious.

One January morning, several of us in the breakfast buffet line were shocked out of our doziness when we observed the owner/manager storm into the dining hall and scream,

	“I told you when you came here. No babies!”

There were no cheerful greetings that January morning when we learned they were pregnant. 

With stunned faces, we busied ourselves with our plates as the young husband and wife, lowered their heads and wordlessly spooned our hot cereal into our bowls.

When their last day came, we patrons, having previously observed the written rules to not tip staff, handed the bride and groom an envelope with enough to get them through three months.

There are three "movements" percolating in Cuba. One consists of the current government and their supporters.

When Fidel was president, Raul was head of the army and national security. When Fidel died and Raul took over, he moved out his brother's people and replaced them with his own.

As heads of government agencies, especially the army and the police, this group desperately seeks to hold on to power and whatever economic advantage political power brings.

The "old guard" who got moved out includes a strong contingent who support reform and others who simply want their positions of power back.

Then there are the various reform movements. They are not unified or particularly well organized. And their visions of reform vary from a complete break with the current economy or some version of a mixed economy, like Vietnam or China.

But they are united around one principle. Power must shift from this family control to the People's Power, the Cuban National Assembly. And a full open debate about the island's future must take place.

While the US gives speeches about democracy and freedom, their model for change is Venezuela, which has become an American colony.

All Cuban's oppose US control but what will happen next is uncertain. But one thing is certain, the blockade continues to impose hardship on the Cuban people.

Halberstam's description of Charlotte Curtis  as a "bright, tough little broad" is not necessarily "casually sexist". 
The first two words are terms of respect, especially in an era where toughness- indicating strength, resilience, and determination - was (and are still) prized in either sex.

"Broad" has become derogatory today, but at the time it was quasi-neutral: many derogatory terms had been co-opted to become terms of respect. 

Notably, the journalist Drew Pearson co-opted the term "muckraker" to denote a serious and dogged investigative reporter. (The term was retrospectively applied to Ida Tarbell, who exposed John D. Rockefeller's shenanigans in growing Standard Oil.) 

Also, in Black culture (as in Isaac Hayes' lyrics in "Theme from Shaft") , the phrase "One Bad MF" was a term of admiration.

In the "hard-boiled" school of detective fiction, e.g.,  Raymond Chandler's Marlowe stories, the term "broad" is used in both a derogatory sense and (occasionally) a respectful one when prefixed by "tough" to indicate a woman who is not necessarily attractive - she's typically middle-aged - but who is resilient and street-smart, even somewhat wise.

Halberstam respected Curtis, referring to her, not facetiously, as ""one of the most powerful MEN on the paper", so I suspect that he, immersed in the culture of his time, was channeling Chandler.

One fact worth mentioning that the article omitted: this was about a 7 on any of the magnitude scales in common use, which is massive, yes.

But the Japan Meteorological Agency also has a “severity” scale that they report, which includes factors such as duration and the type of ground motion and area affected. It is meant to characterize the scale of the damage. Unlike the seismic magnitude scales which are open-ended and logarithmic, the severity scale is fixed at 0-7.

Yesterday’s quake was a 7 on the severity scale.

As bad as it was, I’m still impressed at the limited extent of the damage. This was a bigger quake than what just flattened Venezuela, and I think bigger than those a few years ago in Afghanistan. Here we have a few dead, a dozen missing. That shopping mall collapse is the only major building destroyed. A number of homes have also collapsed … but that number is small. One freight train derailed, but I expect passenger rail service will be mostly restored today. A side-by-side pair of freeway overpasses failed but did not collapse.

You do not want to be anywhere near an earthquake of this scale.

But, if you must be, the only place you want to have to experience it is Japan.

The farther north you go, the bigger the swing between summer and winter daylight becomes. 

At Minnesota’s northern tip, the farthest point north in the contiguous United States, the longest day in June has about seven more hours of sunlight than the shortest day in December. In Key West, that seasonal difference is only about three hours.

Because of this, changes between daylight saving time and standard time have a much stronger impact on people living in northern regions, where the natural daylight shift is already extreme.

The Fed should not attempt to preemptively combat inflation when the concern is moderate inflationary pressure rather than severe, double-digit inflation. Reacting sensitively to every small percentage tick in inflation data could erode public confidence and trust in the Fed and the economy.

One aspect often disregarded in casually calling for short-term interest rate hikes is the reality of credit-heavy national economies and high levels of consumer debt. In addition, without solid anticipation of a plausible trajectory of consistent future rate hikes, raising one-time or sporadic quarter-point rates will likely fail to signal a strong commitment to anchoring inflation expectations among markets and businesses. The only economic impact of such a hike will be to marginally raise costs for everyone without achieving any meaningful policy goals.

In fact, the recent report of rising mortgage rates provides a strong argument for cutting short-term interest rates to spur economic growth and ultimately lower long-term borrowing costs. As for the recent volatility in oil prices, based on my observation, I tend to believe that it was likely driven by opportunistic trading activities through speculative positioning and algorithmic triggers to maximize short-term profits, rather than market fundamentals based on actual supply-demand.

At the present moment, however, given all the variables and uncertainties, I’d also agree that the wait-and-see approach seems prudent and appropriate.

I'm one of 4 couples who have been traveling together for 30 years --- we know how to do it.  It's interesting when others join us and how they think (or don't). 

We split everything -- no exceptions. Some people go nuts with this.  If we are renting a house or villa and we are driving and cooking we bring food and drink for the day we are cooking w/ no accounting. Anything past that gets split if we are staying more than 4 nights for example. If flying -- everything is split. We tip 23% -- no game playing.  We have an accountant in the group and we let her do her thing -- she loves doing it and we love that she does !  One of the guys likes to send out the general list of stuff we need if a driving trip --  we all know by now who's job it is to bring the chips and Vodka but we get the lists anyway.

The typical problem we have is people who say they did not think it would be as costly even with it being what we said it would be.  We did have a strange one. A coupe who had occasionally traveled with us won a Villa for a week at a charity auction (in another country). They invited our group and then later had each coupe kick in the percent had we agreed upfront and booked it ($3200).   They had been involved in two birthday trips  where the Villa was paid for by the birthday couple and a similar charity one where no one paid.  As they say -- always check !

comments.body:
The U.S. should purchase or lease on a long-term basis various types of idle tanker vessels from international shipping companies and seek congressional approval to register them officially as U.S. tankers. These tanker vessels, along with tankers owned by U.S. companies, would be deployed to sail through the strait using the vessels' autonomous navigation systems in coordination with naval security escorts. Throughout the mission, the administration would offer guarantees to provide full compensation in the event of an attack by utilizing Iran's frozen assets, supplemented by the TRIA program. I suspect that the potential profits anticipated from this justifiable quasi-monopoly operation would be more than sufficient to fund this mission.

As for the situation in the Red Sea, perhaps there should be a mention of the fact that U.S. allies have maintained a significant and active naval presence in the Red Sea region for years, primarily tasked with countering Houthi strikes on ships and regional maritime threats.

In addition, it may be worth examining how Iran could find itself in a precarious position if it coordinates with the Houthis on attacks against civilian ships and allied navies in the Red Sea, as such attacks could force U.S. allies to expand their naval operations to the Strait of Hormuz.

In my view, the effectiveness and impact of Houthi threats to blockade the Red Sea may be reassessed more objectively by taking those factors into consideration.
